hero.title: Why am I still single test: 20 in-depth questions
hero.description: You're single, it's been going on for a while, and you don't quite know why. This test looks at your daily life, your encounters and what goes on in your head to find the cause that weighs the most for you, and the one right behind it.
hero.subtitle: Twenty questions, five minutes, and two questions that change depending on your answers

section1.title: The main reasons people stay single
section1.intro: When you've been single for a long time, you often look for a single explanation. In reality there are eight that come up all the time, and most people combine two of them. Here are those eight reasons, in the order they appear in a life: first what prevents the encounter, then what stops it from lasting.
section1.sub1Title: You no longer meet anyone new
section1.sub1P1: This is the most ordinary reason and the most frequent one. Work, home, the same friends, the same places. A week can go by without you exchanging three words with someone you didn't know. Working from home has made this even more common. Nothing wrong with that life, except that an encounter needs raw material: new people, and ideally the same ones several times in a row.
section1.sub1P2: The telltale sign: you can't remember the last time you met someone by chance.
section1.sub2Title: Your social life shrank without you deciding it
section1.sub2P1: Friends get into relationships, have children, move away. Invitations thin out. You don't pick up the slack, because you're tired or because you don't quite know how. After two years, the circle can be counted on one hand, and you mostly talk by message. Long-term singleness often comes from there, far more than from any problem with attraction: most romantic encounters happen indirectly, through friends of friends. Less social life mechanically means fewer encounters.
section1.sub3P1: You see someone you like, you look for the line, you wait for a sign, and the moment passes. It isn't only shyness. It's the fear of rejection weighing more than the wish to find out. Plenty of people who are very much at ease with their friends freeze as soon as something is at stake. And since nobody sees what didn't happen, you walk away telling yourself it wouldn't have worked anyway.
section1.sub4P1: You can have been alone for two years and not be available. An ex you still watch from a distance, a story that hurt too much, and the place is taken. It shows in one detail: everything goes well for three weeks, then you find flaws, you slow down, you drift away. It isn't boredom, it's protection. If you recognise yourself, what happens inside you when an encounter comes along deserves a test of its own.
section1.sub5P1: Age, height, job, city, the way they dress, the humour in the first message. Every criterion can be defended. Put together, they let nobody through. And the love at first sight you're waiting for is rare: many solid couples started with "not bad, worth seeing again". A very precise list often hides something else, by the way. It describes an ex, or it serves to take no risk at all.
section1.sub6P1: When someone good shows interest in you and your first thought is "they'll be disappointed", you start out defeated. You play yourself down, you point out your flaws before anyone sees them, you read every silence as a confirmation. It's not about looks. It's a way of seeing yourself, and it shows. It makes you less available, it makes the other person doubt, and it ends up producing what it feared.
section1.sub7Title: A relationship has no room in your life
section1.sub7P1: You say you want a relationship, and it's probably true. But your diary says otherwise: work, sport, projects and habits take up everything. Someone else would have nowhere to fit. It isn't a flaw, it's a choice you haven't put into words. The problem is the gap between the wish you state and the room there actually is. The people you meet sense it quickly.
section1.sub8P1: Here, encounters happen. What sticks is what comes after. The first date with no follow-up, the conversation that fizzles out, the story that stops after three weeks. Pace is often the culprit: too fast, the other person backs off. Too slow, they conclude there's no interest. Or you wait for them to do everything. Or you look for the detail that's off from the second message. There, it isn't the encounter that needs work, it's the way you let it grow.

section2.title: How do you get out of being single as efficiently as possible?
section2.p1: The answer rarely lies in one more app or one more night out. It lies in your living environment. In the Épic survey by France's national demographic institute Ined, run in 2013 and 2014 among more than 7,000 people, couples mostly formed in the places where people see each other again: evenings with friends, university, work, activities. The internet came far behind, with fewer than one couple in ten. What these places have in common is repetition. You see the same person several weeks running, you talk with nothing at stake, and one day it tips over.
section2.p2: That's no accident. Psychologists measured it long ago: the more you come across someone, the more likely you are to like them. This is the mere exposure effect, described by Robert Zajonc in 1968. And as early as 1950, a study by Leon Festinger in a student housing complex showed that friendships formed first between next-door neighbours, down to a few metres. Love follows roughly the same rule: it grows out of repeated proximity, far more than out of one big night.
section2.p3: So getting out of being single efficiently means changing the shape of your week, not just your Saturday night. Here is what works best, in order.
section2.sub1Title: Add one place where you see the same people again
section2.sub1P1: A class, a team sport, an association, a choir, some volunteering. It doesn't matter what, as long as it's every week and with the same people. One regular activity does more for encounters than ten evenings out where you'll never see anyone again. And even if love isn't there, that's where you rebuild the friends who, in turn, will introduce you to someone.
section2.sub2Title: Say yes a little more often than usual
section2.sub2P1: The invitation you decline because you won't know anyone, the second date you turn down because there was no spark, the colleague who suggests a drink after work. For three months, say yes to what you would have refused out of habit. You won't necessarily meet someone every time. You'll put chance back into a life that had run out of it.
section2.sub3Title: Make the first move, once a week
section2.sub3P1: Not a declaration. One sentence. A remark to someone in a queue, a message after a party, a "shall we do this again?" after a date. Most stories that don't start don't start because nobody said anything. Once a week is enough for it to become a habit, and to discover that the answer is yes far more often than you think.
section2.sub4Title: Use the apps for what they do well
section2.sub4P1: They multiply first contacts, they do nothing more. If you use them, set yourself a rule: as soon as a conversation lasts three exchanges, you suggest a drink. A week of messages doesn't replace twenty minutes face to face. And if they discourage you, stop without guilt: the vast majority of couples met in real life.

section3.title: I'm single and I'm afraid of getting into a relationship: crossing the mental barrier
section3.p1: There is one case where changing your living environment isn't enough: when it's the very idea of a relationship that scares you. It's easy to recognise. Encounters happen, sometimes they go well, and that's precisely where things go wrong. As soon as it gets serious, you find flaws, you reply less, you feel cramped. From the outside, it looks like being demanding. From the inside, it's fear: fear of getting hurt again, fear of losing your freedom, fear of not measuring up once the other person gets to know you.
section3.p2: This fear almost always has an origin. A story that hurt a great deal, parents who tore each other apart, or simply a way of attaching that settled in early and is wary of closeness. The good news is that it isn't crossed in one go, and you don't have to. It's crossed in small steps, with someone patient, by staying one more week each time the urge to leave arrives.
section3.p3: Concretely, three things help. First, put a name on what's happening: the way you attach to people often explains why you pull back, and knowing you're avoidant or anxious already changes how you look at your reactions. Second, tell the person concerned, early and simply: "I tend to pull away when things get serious, it's not about you". That takes the weight of guessing off them. Finally, separate the fear from the decision: being afraid doesn't mean the relationship is bad. It means it matters.
section3.p4: If you want to go further on this specific point, the fear of commitment has its signs, its causes and its ways out, and it concerns far more people than you'd think.

section4.title: What our test calculates
section4.p1: This test doesn't give a mark. It looks for a cause. The twenty questions cover eight precise things: the chances to meet people in your week, your social life, the fear of approaching, a heart still taken by the past or by fear, a filter that's too tight, the way you see yourself, the real room a relationship has in your life, and what happens after the first exchanges.
section4.p2: Each answer weighs on one or two of these causes, with a weight of one to three points depending on what it says. "I think about what I could say, and the moment passes" weighs more on the fear of approaching than "depends on the day". At the end, each cause is brought back to a percentage of what it could have received, so that a cause measured by five questions and a cause measured by three can be compared on the same scale.
section4.p3: Two questions change depending on your answers. If you've never been in a relationship, we ask what, in your view, made it never happen. If you have, we ask where you stand with your last relationship. The same goes for apps: someone who uses them doesn't answer the same question as someone who wants nothing to do with them. Everyone answers twenty questions, but not the same ones.
section4.p4: The result shows the cause that weighs the most, the one right behind it when it weighs almost as much, and the eight bars so you can see the rest. If no cause goes above a certain threshold, the test says so: nothing is blocking you, what's mostly missing is chances. There are no right answers, and nobody sees yours. Answer the way you actually behave, not the way you'd like to.

jsonLd.faq1Q: Why am I single when I'm a good person?
jsonLd.faq1A: Because being a good person isn't enough to bring about an encounter. Most long stretches of being single come down to living environment: you no longer meet anyone new, or the circle of friends has shrunk. Qualities change nothing if nobody is there to see them. That's exactly what this test looks for: the cause that weighs the most for you, so you can act on it rather than doubt yourself.
jsonLd.faq2Q: Is it normal to be single for several years?
jsonLd.faq2A: Yes. The age of the first relationship keeps getting later, break-ups are more frequent, and many people live through several periods of being single in their lives, sometimes long ones. What matters isn't the length, it's whether being single suits you or weighs on you. If it weighs on you, it almost always has a cause that can be named.
jsonLd.faq3Q: I've never been in a relationship at 25 or 30, is that serious?
jsonLd.faq3A: No, and you're less alone than you think. What helps is understanding why it never happened: chances that were missing, a fear of approaching, a doubt about yourself, or simply no wish for it so far. This test asks the question directly to those who have never been in a relationship, and the answer changes the rest of the test.
jsonLd.faq4Q: How do I know if the problem is me?
jsonLd.faq4A: By looking at what happens at each stage. If nobody comes along, the problem is in your week, not in you. If people come along and you don't dare, or you rule them out quickly, or it always stops at the same point, then there's a reflex to work on. That's not the same thing as a flaw: a reflex can be changed.
jsonLd.faq5A: Yes. Your answers stay in your browser, nothing is sent with your name. Only the final result, without any answer or personal data, is counted to know how the causes are spread among the people who take the test.
